messages:
Jamie: Heads-up — saw a cascading warmstart on prod-4 last night after a regional S3 blip. A few shards failed slow on the primary transport, we kicked into the fallback path, and the runtime started parallel warmstarts which evicted the prefix KV cache. Result: token latency spike and ~20% more OOM churn.

Ravi: Can you paste the minimal repro or the logs? Which transport failed first?

Jamie: Logs: 
```
2026-03-19T03:14:08Z shard=shard-84 transport=http2 GET range 0-1mb ok
2026-03-19T03:14:09Z shard=shard-84 transport=s3 range GET timeout 30000ms
2026-03-19T03:14:10Z runtime=worker-7 shard=shard-84 fallback->gcs start
2026-03-19T03:14:11Z shard=shard-84 warmup start parallel=4
2026-03-19T03:14:12Z eviction prefix-kv cache evict_count=162
```
Primary failure was the S3 range endpoint timing out intermittently.

Anya: Ugh. So the runtime starts multiple fallback attempts concurrently for different shards and they all try to read big ranges, saturate IO, and thrash memory cache.

Simon: Sounds like two problems: 1) transport failover strategy is eager and triggers parallel heavy IO, 2) warmup scheduling doesn't account for global backpressure. We should shape failover and add a circuit-breaker per-transport and per-shard.

Jamie: Agreed. Proposal sketch: introduce a ShardLoadPolicy that the loader consults before starting a transport. Policy fields: prefer_streaming (bool), max_failover_attempts (int), sequential_fallback (bool), backoff_ms (int), priority (critical|background). Pseudocode: 
```
if (shard.priority == background) defer warmup by jitter(backoff_ms)
if (transport.is_unhealthy()) try next transport sequentially with backoff
cap parallel_warmups globally = min(pool_size/2, 8)
```

Ravi: I like sequential_fallback=true by default. But we need a rule for mixed-format bundles (safetensors+quant shards) — do we treat header reads as cheap and always do header-only probes?

Simon: Yes. Cheap header probe first: read first few KB of safetensors header (or index), decide transport viability. If header comes back successful, then either mmap/range or stream based on size and health metrics. Also: prefer mmap/range for >128MB shards, stream for <8MB. Middle sizes use heuristics.

Anya: Implementation complexity concern: we already have transport adapters for http, s3, gs, local. Adding per-transport circuit state + header probes will complicate the loader interface. Suggest we define a small stable interface: 
```
TransportProbeResult probe(transport, shard_id) -> {healthy: bool, latency_ms: int, supports_range: bool}
TransportPolicy choose(ProbeResults...) -> prioritized list
```
Keep the loader agnostic beyond probe + prioritized transport list.

Maya: Rollout question — how do we safely deploy? The last time a change to warmup scheduling regressed tail latencies on Dedicated.

Jamie: Canary: enable policy for 1% of requests on hosted, 5% on a dedicated pool, monitor warmup_latency_p50/p95, failover_count, prefix_kv_evictions. If metrics look good for 48h, ramp.

Ravi: Also add a quick fail-safe: if global prefix_kv_evictions > threshold within 5m, flip runtime to "fail-fast" mode where heavy warmups are serialized and small shards served from fallback tiny model. That buy us breathing room.

Simon: Another edge: quantized shards sometimes require index-first hydration (we can't stream into quant loader easily). For those, the policy should set preload_kv=true and be stricter on transport health before attempting.

Anya: Agree. Need tests: unit test probe behavior, integration sim that injects transport latency/timeouts, and a load test that simulates partial region outage to validate no cascading OOMs.

Kai-bot: Deploy-checklist added: rfc/shard-transport-failover.md, canary flags, dashboard panels for shard.failovers, runtime.eviction_events.

Jamie: Action items: 1) Simon + Anya to draft the TransportProbe API and ShardLoadPolicy config (this week). 2) Ravi + Maya to design canary metrics and alert thresholds. 3) Jamie to add quick fail-safe toggle.

Maya: lgtm. Add a short README for operators explaining the new flags and what to do when eviction alarms fire. :thumbsup:

Ravi: One more: consider a "graceful degrade" path — if too many concurrent warmups then runtime routes requests to a smaller-sequence model (or short-circuits to cached responses) instead of trying more fallbacks. That might be much safer than aggressive retry.

Jamie: Noted. We'll evaluate as a last-resort emergency fallback. Thanks all — I'll open the RFC follow-up PR with the policy schema and tests. :facepalm:
